# The Teaching of the Buddhas

*Dhp 179-196, the Buddhavagga — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 3 min · 459 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This chapter of the Dhammapada is about the Buddha: what it means that he
appeared, and what he taught.

It contains the verse many people treat as the whole teaching in four lines:
*not doing any evil, taking up the wholesome, purifying your own mind: this
is the teaching of the Buddhas.* The verses around it fill in the daily
shape of that: patience, not harming anyone, moderation in eating, a quiet
place to sit, and devotion to the higher mind.

Later verses ask what a real refuge is. Frightened people take refuge in
mountains, forests, and shrines. The refuge that works is the Buddha, the
Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and the text defines it by what you see: the four
noble truths.

The numbers beside the verses are the Dhammapada's own verse numbers.

## Translation

### Verses

<span class="verse-number">179</span><span class="verse-line">Whose victory cannot be undone,</span>
<span class="verse-line">whose victory no one in the world can follow:</span>
<span class="verse-line">that Buddha, whose range has no end,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">who leaves no track, by what track will you lead him?</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">180</span><span class="verse-line">In whom there is no ignorant wanting,</span>
<span class="verse-line">that net, that entanglement, to lead him anywhere:</span>
<span class="verse-line">that Buddha, whose range has no end,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">who leaves no track, by what track will you lead him?</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">181</span><span class="verse-line">The steadfast, intent on the mental themes,</span>
<span class="verse-line">delighting in the calm of renunciation,</span>
<span class="verse-line">fully awakened, remembering:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">even the devas envy them.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">182</span><span class="verse-line">Hard it is to be born human,</span>
<span class="verse-line">hard the life of mortals,</span>
<span class="verse-line">hard to hear the true Dhamma,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">hard the arising of Buddhas.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">183</span><span class="verse-line">Not doing any evil,</span>
<span class="verse-line">taking up the wholesome,</span>
<span class="verse-line">purifying your own mind:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">this is the teaching of the Buddhas.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">184</span><span class="verse-line">Patience, enduring patience, is the highest austerity;</span>
<span class="verse-line">nibbāna is the highest, the Buddhas say.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Someone who harms another has not gone forth;</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">someone who troubles another is no samaṇa.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">185</span><span class="verse-line">Not blaming, not harming,</span>
<span class="verse-line">restraint in the pāṭimokkha,</span>
<span class="verse-line">moderation in eating,</span>
<span class="verse-line">a secluded place to sleep and sit,</span>
<span class="verse-line">and devotion to the higher mind:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">this is the teaching of the Buddhas.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">186</span><span class="verse-line">Not with a shower of coins</span>
<span class="verse-line">is there contentment in sensuality.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Sensuality gives little gratification and much pain:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">knowing this, the wise</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">187</span><span class="verse-line">find no delight</span>
<span class="verse-line">even in heavenly sensuality.</span>
<span class="verse-line">The disciple of the fully awakened Buddha</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">delights in the ending of ignorant wanting.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">188</span><span class="verse-line">People driven by fear</span>
<span class="verse-line">go for refuge to many things:</span>
<span class="verse-line">to mountains and forests,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">to parks, trees, and shrines.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">189</span><span class="verse-line">That is not a secure refuge,</span>
<span class="verse-line">that is not the highest refuge.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Going to that refuge,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">no one is released from all dissatisfaction.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">190</span><span class="verse-line">But whoever has gone for refuge</span>
<span class="verse-line">to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha</span>
<span class="verse-line">sees with right discernment</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">the four noble truths:</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">191</span><span class="verse-line">dissatisfaction, the arising of dissatisfaction,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the going beyond dissatisfaction,</span>
<span class="verse-line">and the noble eightfold path</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">that leads to the calming of dissatisfaction.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">192</span><span class="verse-line">That is the secure refuge,</span>
<span class="verse-line">that is the highest refuge.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Going to that refuge,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">you are released from all dissatisfaction.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">193</span><span class="verse-line">A thoroughbred among people is hard to find,</span>
<span class="verse-line">and is not born just anywhere.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Wherever that steadfast person is born,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">that family prospers in happiness.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">194</span><span class="verse-line">Happy is the arising of Buddhas,</span>
<span class="verse-line">happy the teaching of the true Dhamma,</span>
<span class="verse-line">happy the harmony of the Saṅgha,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">happy the austerity of those in harmony.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">195</span><span class="verse-line">Whoever honors those worthy of honor,</span>
<span class="verse-line">whether Buddhas or their disciples,</span>
<span class="verse-line">who have gone beyond proliferation</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">and crossed over sorrow and lamentation,</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">196</span><span class="verse-line">whoever honors such ones,</span>
<span class="verse-line">cooled and fearing nothing from any side:</span>
<span class="verse-line">no one can measure their benefit</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">by saying it is this much.</span>
{: .verse }

The fourteenth chapter, on the Buddha, is finished.

<summary>Words used in this translation (15)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>calming</dfn></dt>
<dd>A settling and quieting of the mind on the way toward full release.</dd>
<dt><dfn>crossed over</dfn></dt>
<dd>Having completed the crossing rather than merely moving toward the other side. This preserves the river image used for completion of the path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Dhamma</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddha&#x27;s teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dissatisfaction</dfn></dt>
<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>gratification</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;assāda&quot;: the real satisfaction something offers, which is why people hold on to it. The texts pair it with that thing&#x27;s danger and the escape from it, so you see all three together.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorant wanting</dfn></dt>
<dd>Wanting something you can&#x27;t have right now. This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;taṇhā&quot;, often translated &quot;craving&quot;. We call it ignorant because it comes from not seeing clearly; ordinary, sensible wanting is something else.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>nibbāna</dfn></dt>
<dd>The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; &quot;quenching&quot; is the closest one-word gloss.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble eightfold path</dfn></dt>
<dd>The eight-part practice these texts teach: right view, right attitude, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right remembering, and right unification of mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>refuge</dfn></dt>
<dd>Where someone turns for safety and direction. Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha is how a person shows they take this path seriously. It is not a conversion ritual.</dd>
<dt><dfn>remembering</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;sati&quot;. It means actively keeping what matters in mind and coming back to it when you lose it. It is not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.</dd>
<dt><dfn>right discernment</dfn></dt>
<dd>Seeing accurately how something actually came about, rather than holding a correct opinion about it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Saṅgha</dfn></dt>
<dd>The community of the Buddha&#x27;s disciples. In traditional recollection formulas, as in AN 11.12, it means especially those who have entered and realized the path, not everyone who calls themselves Buddhist.</dd>
<dt><dfn>wholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;kusala&quot;. Roughly: mentally and ethically healthy. It is blameless, leads to well-being, and people with good judgment praise it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world</dfn></dt>
<dd>A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world we build through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense it has.</dd>
</dl>

*[calming]: A settling and quieting of the mind on the way toward full release.
*[crossed over]: Having completed the crossing rather than merely moving toward the other side. This preserves the river image used for completion of the path.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[dissatisfaction]: This translation's rendering of "dukkha," the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated "suffering," but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.
*[gratification]: This project's rendering of "assāda": the real satisfaction something offers, which is why people hold on to it. The texts pair it with that thing's danger and the escape from it, so you see all three together.
*[ignorant wanting]: Wanting something you can't have right now. This project's rendering of "taṇhā", often translated "craving". We call it ignorant because it comes from not seeing clearly; ordinary, sensible wanting is something else.
*[knowing]: This project's rendering of "viññāṇa" (often translated "consciousness") -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.
*[nibbāna]: The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; "quenching" is the closest one-word gloss.
*[noble eightfold path]: The eight-part practice these texts teach: right view, right attitude, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right remembering, and right unification of mind.
*[refuge]: Where someone turns for safety and direction. Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha is how a person shows they take this path seriously. It is not a conversion ritual.
*[remembering]: This project's rendering of "sati". It means actively keeping what matters in mind and coming back to it when you lose it. It is not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.
*[right discernment]: Seeing accurately how something actually came about, rather than holding a correct opinion about it.
*[Saṅgha]: The community of the Buddha's disciples. In traditional recollection formulas, as in AN 11.12, it means especially those who have entered and realized the path, not everyone who calls themselves Buddhist.
*[wholesome]: This project's rendering of "kusala". Roughly: mentally and ethically healthy. It is blameless, leads to well-being, and people with good judgment praise it.
*[world]: A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world we build through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense it has.
